Only what's in their pockets.
They can all understand each other, and that's the only magic.
The rocks, the plants, the physics: all painfully real.
The scientists are real people.
What they say and do here is our invention.
So who takes charge?
And who panics first?
Day one, late morning.
A hundred brilliant people.
A hundred different ideas of what to do first.
For a whole hour, nothing useful happens.
Then Fridtjof Nansen, the man who crossed Greenland on skis, asks the one question that matters.
Can anyone here make fire without matches?
Two hands go up.
Halfway.
Two!
Out of a hundred.
And both of them look unsure.

lines.text: Hmm.
Somebody has to take over.
Benjamin Franklin does, naturally.
One rule: every group reports at a nightly meeting, and anyone can stop work for safety.
Even Newton agrees.
Somebody write that down.
But a rule won't keep anyone warm.
And the sun is already sinking.

lines.text: So, the order.
Warmth first.
Then water.
Then food.
Alfred Russel Wallace finds a spring, right where the water leaves the ground.
And John Snow, yes, that John Snow, adds the rule that will save lives for months.
Latrines go downstream.
Never near the spring.
Uh-oh.
Then the wind changes.

lines.text: The sun drops, the wind picks up, and the real danger arrives.
It isn't freezing.
It's cold, wind and damp clothes, all at once.
So they build a windbreak of branches and pile dry grass against it.
Why grass?
Because trapped air is the oldest insulation there is.
It buys them time.
But only fire buys them the night.
Now.
Fire.
Nansen tries a bow drill.
A dozen tries.
Sore hands.
Nothing but smoke.
Franklin keeps the tinder dry, and waits.
Then Einstein takes off his reading glasses.
Oh.
A convex lens.
The afternoon sun.
One bright point on the grass.
A thread of smoke.
One careful breath... and fire!
But can they keep it alive?

lines.text: Well, the hard part isn't making it.
It's keeping it.
Franklin once founded a volunteer fire company, so he sets a night watch, in shifts.
Which leaves one question.
What's for dinner?
Almost nothing.
A few nuts, some eggs, raw wild grain.
Darwin and Wallace refuse to gamble on plants they don't know.
Wise.
Out here, one wrong guess can poison you.
And they still have to sleep.
One spring.
One fire.
One windbreak.
One rule.
Nobody has invented anything.
They spent the whole day doing what a ten-year-old hunter-gatherer could do.
Slower.
And with more opinions.
And tomorrow?
Tomorrow, they need a pot.
Could a hundred of history's greatest minds survive a week of this?
Day seven.
Franklin runs a census.
On bark. With charcoal.
Column one: who has done this before?
Six names.
Column two: who has ever chipped a flint?
Four.
Everybody else knows exactly WHY things work.
They've just never done any of them.
Ninety brilliant theories, and no calluses.
But scientists have one superpower.
They don't guess. They TEST.
And the first test is lunch.
Because a hundred adults need about two hundred and fifty thousand calories.
Every. Day.
Luckily, wild einkorn grows right there on the hillside.
So Wallace picks up a flint sickle and starts cutting.
About two kilograms an hour.
Nansen does the sum.
To feed everyone, that's seventy-five kilograms of grain. A day.
By the end of the week, a third of the colony does nothing but grain.
And cutting grain needs sharp stone. So who knows stone?
Nobody, except Darwin. He started out as a geologist, and he spots white lumps in the limestone.
Flint!
Newton hits a flint. The flint wins.
By day four, they have a heap of flakes, scrapers and crude axes.
But the real leap is hafting.
Einstein mixes pine resin with charcoal, and it turns into glue.
Then wet sinew is wrapped around the joint. As it dries, it SHRINKS, and the head locks tight.
Now they have axes. Which means somebody can finally build something.
Newton and Franklin design only what wood and stone allow.
Tesla sketches something much grander.
Curie looks at it. Then at the pile of logs. Then at him.
The problem? There is no metal. Not for a pin, not for an axle. Only wood.
They try anyway.
SNAP.
The wooden pin breaks. The log rolls. Everybody dives.
Franklin is, technically, still alive.
Design is easy. Materials are HARD.
And tonight there's an even bigger problem. The water is making people sick.
John Snow has one rule: boil it.
But there's no pot.
Day one promised one. Day one was optimistic.
So they dig a pit, line it with hide, and drop in stones that have sat in the fire.
Hiss. Steam. It works.
Until a stone explodes.
Wet river cobbles hold water inside. Heat them, and the rock bursts.
Shrapnel. Several small cuts. Everybody learns something, mostly about shrapnel.
Then Curie makes soap, from animal fat and wood ash.
It smells awful. Nobody likes the smell. Everybody likes not dying.
But the sun is already going down.
And that's day seven.
A secure camp. A stock of stone tools. A water routine.
Two people are sick. One cut is infected. One wrist is broken.
Nansen looks at the dark valley, and at the hills beyond.
Because the one thing they can't chop, grind or boil is time.
And a winter is coming.
And a month from now?
Somebody finally invents the POT.
Day thirty.
The pot!
Which is awkward, because the oldest pottery we know of is already eight thousand years old.
In China. Not here. The people living nearby won't have a single pot for another three thousand years.
So Marie Curie goes looking for clay.
River clay, chopped straw, a little sand.
Why the straw? Because plain clay shrinks as it dries, and then it cracks.
Seven pots. Seven explosions.
Newton looks at the pieces. Then he does what Newton does.
He measures.
Dry them slowly. Heat them slowly. Bury them in a pit, and cover the pit with glowing wood.
Eleven days later, one pot holds water.
And then, at last, there is soup.
Nobody has ever been so moved by soup.
Day thirty-three.
A column of smoke rises from the next ridge.
Not theirs.
Somebody else lives here.
Hunters have lived in this country for thousands of years. Within a few hundred, people like these will raise the oldest stone temple we know: Göbekli Tepe, not far from here.
There's one small problem. The magic that lets the hundred understand each other doesn't work on anybody else.
So Franklin tries diplomacy. He holds out a pot.
The hunters look at the pot. They look at Franklin. Then one of them knocks on it, listens, and says something that, in any language, means: how much?
The first deal in the colony's history: one pot, for a haunch of gazelle.
And that changes everything. A hundred adults are a camp. A people needs more.
But winter is nearly here. Will they have a village by spring, or a graveyard?
Spring.
Not everybody sees it.
The first winter takes five of the hundred. A fever, a bad tooth, a fall on the ice.
That number is our invention, but not a wild one: hunter-gatherers lose a few adults in every hundred each year.
John Snow writes down the causes in charcoal, on bark.
And one thing is different from the cave-man winters you've seen. Nobody died of the water.
Now it's Darwin's turn.
He clears a patch of ground beside the camp and sows wild einkorn from the seed they saved.
And here's the twist. Wild wheat is generous.
In the nineteen-sixties, the botanist Jack Harlan cut wild wheat by hand in these same hills, with a stone-bladed sickle. His estimate: a family could gather a year's grain in about three weeks.
So why farm at all?
Darwin has the answer. A hundred people can't live on wild wheat in one place. They'd strip the hillside bare in a single season.
Then Darwin does the cleverest thing anyone does all year.
Wild wheat has a flaw, from a farmer's point of view. When an ear is ripe, it shatters, and the grain falls to the ground.
But every so often, one plant holds on to its grain.
Darwin saves only those. Every harvest. Year after year.
In the real world, say the archaeologists, wheat took a thousand to two thousand years to change like this.
Some computer models say it could happen in twenty to a hundred years, if you choose the seed on purpose.
Who's right? Nobody knows.
But the biggest event of year one isn't wheat.
It's a baby.
And with babies comes a problem nobody planned for.
A hundred adults can survive a winter. But can they keep every skill alive?
One famous study argues that when rising seas cut off Tasmania, its four thousand people slowly lost bone tools, warm clothing, even fishing. Other researchers disagree.
A hundred people is a lot smaller than four thousand.
So Franklin calls a meeting. Everyone teaches. Everyone writes.
Writing doesn't exist yet. Not for another sixty-seven hundred years.
These people brought it with them.
They press signs into wet clay, then bake the tablets in the new kiln. Fire doesn't destroy them. It saves them.
The colony's first library. Knowledge, backed up.
But writing down a recipe isn't the same as cooking it.
So ten years from now, can they make metal?
Year ten.
The first children are ten years old, and every one of them can read.
Which makes them the best-educated ten-year-olds on Earth, and the rudest.
The colony is bigger now: about a hundred and thirty people, counting neighbours who married in. That's our estimate.
And everybody stares at the same problem. Stone tools break.
Metal doesn't.
Marie Curie has found a green rock in the next valley.
Malachite.
Crush it. Mix it with charcoal. Put it in the hottest kiln they own, and blow air through a hide bellows.
Hours later the ash breaks open, and there it is: a small red-gold bead of copper.
Near here, people will begin hammering raw lumps of copper into beads within a thousand years or so. Real smelting? That's five thousand years away.
Then Tesla asks the question nobody wants to hear. So where does the electricity come in?
Not now, Nikola.
But copper is soft. A copper axe bends where a stone axe would chip.
Bronze is harder. Bronze is copper plus tin.
And tin is the problem. It's rare, and there's almost none of it near here.
Archaeologists still argue about where the ancient Near East found its tin.
A hundred of the cleverest people in history, defeated by one silvery metal that isn't there.
So Curie suggests skipping bronze. Go straight to iron.
Iron ore is everywhere: whole hills the colour of rust.
But iron needs a furnace well over a thousand degrees, and a mountain of charcoal.
In modern experiments, a block of iron under two kilograms swallows about forty kilograms of charcoal.
A single knife costs a forest.
Real humans took until about twelve hundred BCE to make iron an everyday metal.
Can the hundred beat that? Let's see what a century does.
Year one hundred.
Nobody who arrived on Day One is alive.
Not Newton. Not Curie. Not even the stubborn ones.
How many people live here now? Probably between one and three thousand. If the colony grew three percent a year, it's about nineteen hundred. But growth like that never lasts.
So what did a hundred geniuses leave behind?
Wheat that holds on to its grain. Almost.
Copper tools. A kiln at every door.
A school with a library of four thousand clay tablets.
And one strange custom. Every child boils their water, and nobody remembers why.
It's a rule from the old spirits.
Franklin is now the spirit of thrift. Newton is the grumpy ghost of levers.
And the neighbours? They learned pottery from the colony. The next valley learned it from them.
Because ideas don't spread by magic. They travel with people who meet.
So did the hundred beat history?
Now let's check the real record.
Wheat that no longer drops its grain: a thousand to two thousand years.
Writing: six thousand seven hundred years from this valley.
Copper smelting: five thousand.
Everyday iron: eight thousand eight hundred.
The hundred did writing on Day One. Smelting by year ten.
So yes, knowledge is a time machine. For discoveries.
But discovery was never the only cost.
People.
In ten thousand BCE the whole planet holds about four million. By eighteen hundred, nearly a billion.
More people, more ideas: the economist Michael Kremer built a famous model of exactly that.
Materials. No tin.
Fuel. Forty kilograms of charcoal for one small block of iron.
And tools that make tools. James Watt waited years for someone who could bore a steam cylinder true. John Wilkinson finally did it in seventeen seventy-four.
Then there's trade. A famous essay called I, Pencil points out that no single person on Earth knows how to make a pencil.
The wood, the graphite, the rubber, the brass: all from people who never meet.
A hundred geniuses is not a civilization.
So here's our verdict.
Early on, the hundred beat history. Farming, writing, metal: in centuries, not millennia. We'd bet on that.
Then they hit the wall.
They could fail three ways. A bad winter. A plague. Or the Tasmania problem, skills dying faster than children can learn them.
Or they could win in a quieter way. Shortcut the first ten thousand years, and the world reaches the steam engine in maybe half the time. That's a guess, not a fact.
Real history took eleven thousand seven hundred years to get from this valley to the first working steam engine, and nearly twelve thousand to penicillin.
Which would you bet on? The hundred, or the winter?
Tell me below.
And tell me which two worlds should collide next.
